problem: DRL-based indoor exploration agents rely on dense extrinsic rewards (e.g. occupancy anticipation) that need ground-truth layouts of training environments, while intrinsic rewards (curiosity, novelty, coverage) vanish over the episode. Impact-based rewards had only been used in procedurally generated, countable-state environments.
motivation: Layout ground truth is expensive to obtain and depends on the mapping phase. A stable, purely intrinsic reward would allow training exploration policies without it. In photorealistic continuous environments, exact visitation counts are meaningless because states are almost never revisited, so the count discount must be replaced.
key_idea: Reward the global exploration policy with the impact (L2 change in encoded consecutive RGB observations) discounted by a pseudo-visitation count, obtained either from a spatial grid or from a PixelCNN density model's prediction gain.
insight: A purely intrinsic reward can match or beat extrinsic anticipation reward computed from GT layouts. The count-only ablations (Count Grid / DME) are clearly worse than Impact, e.g. Gibson Val T=500 IoU 0.714/0.764 vs 0.803/0.800, so the impact numerator matters. DME helps more in larger environments (MP3D Test AS 144.64 vs 130.98 for Grid), while Grid gives better pose accuracy and IoU in small scenes.
method: Mapper: CNN takes RGB-D and outputs a 2-channel (occupied/explored) anticipation local map V=101 (5 cm cells), registered into a global map W=961 (Gibson) or 2001 (MP3D).
Pose Estimator: predicts displacement from three modality-specific estimates (RGB, depth, local map) aggregated by softmax-weighted sum; agent actions are forward 0.25 m and turn ±10°.

Hierarchical navigation: PPO global policy samples a goal on an H=240 map every η=25 steps; an A* planner gives local goals within 1.25 m; a PPO local policy outputs discrete actions with a distance-reduction reward.
Impact reward: r = ||φ(s_{t+1})-φ(s_t)||_2 / sqrt(N̂(s_{t+1})) using RGB observation encodings, with an episodic count.
Grid pseudo-count: the global map is divided into G×G cells (G=5 best) and the visit count of the agent's current cell is used, ignoring orientation.

DME pseudo-count: a lightweight Gated PixelCNN on 42×42 grayscale observations quantized to B bins (B=128 best) is trained online across all environments. Count = max{(e^{c·n^-1/2·PG+}-1)^-1, 1}, with c=0.1 and PG clipped at 0.

setting.backbone: Modular DRL agent: CNN mapper, pose estimator and PPO global/local policies, plus a lightweight Gated PixelCNN density model (all trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Gibson train split, 40 parallel environments, ~5M frames, in the Habitat simulator; no extra data
setting.observation: egocentric 128×128 RGB-D (plus noisy odometry/pose estimated by the agent)
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: forward 0.25 m, turn left/right 10°; global policy picks map goal
setting.privileged: none at test time (GT layout is used only for evaluation metrics; the noise-free PointGoal setting uses oracle pose)

numbers_note: Exploration benchmarks have no canonical name in the list, so they are given as other:. Exploration metrics are IoU (fraction), Acc/AS in m², TE in m, AE in degrees. Only the main variants are listed; the FIoU/OIoU/FAS/OAS columns are omitted. PointNav SR/SPL are converted to percent (0.969 → 96.9, etc.), so they are not verbatim printed values.
results: Impact-based agents beat curiosity, coverage, count-based and the extrinsic Anticipation baseline on most exploration metrics. For example, on MP3D Test T=1000 Impact (Grid) reaches IoU 0.502 vs 0.484 for Anticipation, and Impact (DME) reaches AS 212.0. On PointGoal with a noisy pose sensor they reach SR 92.3 (Grid), above Anticipation's 88.5. In the noise-free setting they are on par with the baselines (SR ~96.7–96.9).
limitations: Discrete low-level actions only; continuous velocity control is left out of scope.
Pseudo-count hyperparameters (G, B, c) need tuning, and DME has worse pose error (TE/AE) than Grid; the Grid variant is applicable only when the state is a robot location.
Real-world evaluation is only qualitative (video), with no quantitative results.
builds_on: Pseudo-count (Bellemare et al.; Ostrovski et al.)
